questions.question_text: Which one of the following is false?

options.text: Carl Jung focused on the growth of the personality and individuation
Harry Stack Sullivan saw human development as a function of social interaction
Erik Erikson developed a model of the life cycle that spanned from childhood to old age
Jean Piaget developed a theory of cognitive development
The work of Freud, Jung, and Erikson was a function of carefully crafted psychological and neurodevelopmental studies

correct_answer.text: The work of Freud, Jung, and Erikson was a function of carefully crafted psychological and neurodevelopmental studies

correct_answers.text: The work of Freud, Jung, and Erikson was a function of carefully crafted psychological and neurodevelopmental studies

questions.explanation: There are several life-cycle theorists who are important to know. Freud's theory of development involving oral, anal, and phallic stages is important. Carl Jung felt that development of the personality occurs through experiences that teach a person who they intrinsically are. For him, libido included sexual energy but also spiritual urges and a drive to understand the meaning of life. Harry Stack Sullivan focused on social interaction. In his theory he defined each stage of life through the need to interact with certain individuals. These interactions shaped the development of the personality. Erik Erikson developed a life cycle from childhood to adulthood. It consists of: Stage 1: Trust vs mistrust (Birth to 1 year); Stage 2: Autonomy vs shame and doubt (Ages 1 to 3 years); Stage 3: Initiative vs guilt (Ages 3 to 5 years); Stage 4: Industry vs inferiority (Ages 6 to 11 years); Stage 5: Ego identity vs role confusion (Ages 11 years to end of adolescence); Stage 6: Intimacy vs isolation (Ages 21 to 40 years); Stage 7: Generativity vs stagnation (Ages 40 to 65 years); Stage 8: Ego identity vs despair (Ages 65+ years). Piaget developed a theory of cognitive development consisting of four stages: sensorimotor, preoperational thought, concrete operations, and formal operations. The work of Freud, Jung, and Erikson was the result of observations of children, not carefully crafted studies, and is a framework to understand development but not intended to describe objective reality.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with an acute onset of right hemisensory loss, mild right hemiparesis, and a right-sided Babinski sign. Upon examination of her mental status you note that she cannot repeat simple phrases; she can follow simple task instructions both verbal and on paper; she cannot write well; and she is having word-finding difficulties with multiple paraphasic errors. This clinical picture is consistent with:
questions.explanation: The clinical picture given is that of a conduction aphasia. Conduction aphasia results from left-hemispheric (dominant) lesions, particularly in the inferior parietal or superior temporal regions. The area of predilection is the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas. It is characterized by inability to repeat relatively normal, spontaneous speech, possible paraphasic errors and hesitancy; naming may be impaired but auditory comprehension is intact; writing may or may not be impaired; associated symptoms may include right hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, hemianopsia, and limb apraxia. Broca's aphasia involves a lesion in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus, resulting in broken, stuttering, staccato speech with inability to repeat and phonemic/paraphasic errors; reading often impaired, comprehension usually intact; frequently associated with depression and right hemiparesis/hemisensory loss. Wernicke's aphasia results from a lesion in the superior temporal gyrus; speech is fluent but comprehension impaired, may be logorrheic, with paragrammatism, neologisms, paraphasic errors, and jargon; repetition, naming, and comprehension impaired; often accompanied by right homonymous hemianopsia with absence of motor/sensory signs. Global aphasia results from large lesions involving superior temporal, inferior frontal, and parietal lobes, corresponding to MCA territory; speech nonfluent/mute, comprehension impaired, naming/reading/repetition/writing all poor, with dense right hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, hemianopsia. Transcortical aphasias involve areas around Broca's and Wernicke's areas with repetition spared: transcortical motor aphasia resembles Broca's with sparing of comprehension and fluent repetition (anterior cerebral artery territory); transcortical sensory aphasia resembles Wernicke's with normal repetition (temporo-occipital lesion); transcortical mixed aphasia (isolation of speech area) presents as global aphasia with echolalic repetition only, localizing to watershed areas.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a goal of collaborative care between psychiatry and primary care physicians?
questions.explanation: Collaborative care models seek to expand access to psychiatric treatment to the many primary care patients who would otherwise not be able to gain access to a psychiatrist. Patients are more comfortable being seen in a primary care setting than in the mental health clinic. Treatment is improved when primary care physicians and psychiatrists work together, leading to better diagnosis and more effective treatment regimens. Studies support improved outcomes for patients treated with collaborative care. Improved communication is an important factor that contributes to better overall outcomes. Formularies are determined by the patient's insurance, not by the primary care physician or psychiatrist, so they are not affected by the collaborative care model. However, having the support of the psychiatrist often helps the primary care physician select medications from the patient's formulary that are appropriate for their condition and covered by insurance as well.

questions.question_text: Correcting hyponatremia too rapidly with hypertonic saline replacement can result in:
questions.explanation: The classic complication of rapid sodium replacement in hyponatremia is central pontine myelinolysis. This can result in a clinical transection of the pons and a locked-in syndrome. Locked-in syndrome is the result of a pontine lesion that is clinically devastating and produces quadriplegia, mutism, and a lower cranial nerve palsy that leaves a patient with only the ability to move the eyes up and down and blink the eyelids. Only the upper brainstem function is preserved, and patients usually need to be on a respirator. Cognition and comprehension are usually grossly intact, and the patient is often quite aware of the predicament. Prognosis is very poor. The locked-in syndrome is most often the result of a ventral pontine infarct as a consequence of basilar artery thrombosis but can in certain instances result from central pontine myelinolysis, which produces a more central pontine lesion. Other possible causes of locked-in syndrome are acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome), myasthenia gravis, and neuromuscular blocking agents.

questions.question_text: A patient comes into your office and explains away why he beat his brother with a baseball bat. He gives several examples of how his brother had mistreated him in the past and says that if he had not given him this beating, the mistreatment would have continued. Which of the following defenses does this represent?
questions.explanation: This question contains an example of rationalization. Rationalization is characterized by offering rational explanations in an attempt to justify attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors that may otherwise be unacceptable. Projection is perceiving and reacting to unacceptable inner impulses as if they are outside the self. Blocking is temporarily halting thinking, often occurring in psychosis due to hallucinations and thought disorganization. Externalization is perceiving elements of your own personality in the external world or objects, a more general term than projection. Denial is avoiding awareness of some painful aspect of reality by negating sensory data. The most primitive defenses are the narcissistic defenses (denial, distortion, projection). The least primitive are the mature defenses (altruism, anticipation, asceticism, humor, sublimation, suppression).

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old obese African American woman presents to the emergency room with a complaint of 6 weeks of intermittent bifrontal headache and vague visual obscurations. She is on oral contraceptive medication and has a history of being on tetracycline therapy for a recent sexually transmitted disease. The immediate diagnostic test of choice in the emergency room is:

options.text: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without gadolinium

correct_answer.text: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure

correct_answers.text: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure

questions.explanation: The clinical condition depicted is pseudotumor cerebri, also called benign intracranial hypertension. Classically seen in young, obese, African American women; the exact etiology is unknown. Risk factors include hypervitaminosis A, high-dose corticosteroid therapy, tetracycline therapy, oral contraceptive use, and head trauma. Patients typically present with a waxing and waning headache and intermittent visual obscurations. Neurologic exam can reveal papilledema and enlargement of the blind spot on visual field testing. Brain imaging is usually normal, though some scans reveal slit-like ventricles. Diagnosis is established by lumbar puncture with opening pressure elevated over 20 cm H2O. Treatment of choice is pharmacologic (acetazolamide or prednisone); some patients opt for repeated lumbar punctures. Surgical options include ventriculoperitoneal or lumboperitoneal shunting and optic nerve sheath fenestration. ESR is used diagnostically for temporal arteritis, not this condition. Serum prolactin is sometimes drawn after a seizure to determine if it is epileptic (elevated greater than twice normal within an hour after a true epileptic seizure).

questions.question_text: Which of the following organizations is made up of family members of the mentally ill?

options.text: National Alliance for the Mentally Ill
Association for the Advancement of Psychotherapy

correct_answer.text: National Alliance for the Mentally Ill

correct_answers.text: National Alliance for the Mentally Ill

questions.explanation: The National Alliance for the Mentally Ill (NAMI) is an advocacy group made up of families of the mentally ill that works at local, state, and federal levels to improve services for the mentally ill. They are involved with lawmakers, outreach, and education. The other answer choices are distractors. The most important organization to know is NAMI.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a diagnostic criterion of migraine without aura?
questions.explanation: The criteria for migraine without aura are: at least five headache attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours (untreated or unsuccessfully treated) that have at least two of four characteristics: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate or severe intensity, or aggravated by walking stairs or similar routine physical activity. During the headache at least one of the following occurs: phonophobia and photophobia, or nausea/vomiting. Migraine with aura involves at least two attacks with at least three of: one or more fully reversible aura symptoms indicating focal cerebral cortical/brainstem function; at least one aura symptom develops gradually over more than 4 minutes, or two or more symptoms occur in succession; no aura symptom lasts more than 60 minutes; or headache follows aura with free interval of at least 60 minutes (may also begin with the aura). At least one of the following aura features establishes migraine with typical aura: homonymous visual disturbance, unilateral paresthesias/numbness, unilateral weakness, or aphasia/unclassifiable speech difficulty.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia is 1%. It is estimated that there are somewhere in the vicinity of 2 million patients with schizophrenia in the United States. The other answer choices are distractors.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a contraindication to the use of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (r-TPA) in acute ischemic stroke?

options.text: Stroke occurrence 2 hours before r-TPA administration
Major surgery within 2 weeks of r-TPA administration
CT shows signs of intracranial hemorrhage

correct_answer.text: Stroke occurrence 2 hours before r-TPA administration

correct_answers.text: Stroke occurrence 2 hours before r-TPA administration

questions.explanation: r-TPA is used for acute thrombolysis of ischemic cerebrovascular accidents within 3 hours of the occurrence of the event for most patients and 4.5 hours for select patients. Contraindications to r-TPA include major surgery within the past 14 days, blood pressure over 185/110 mm Hg, bleeding parameters falling outside a narrow range (PT > 15 or INR > 1.7), or a CT showing signs of intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is based on active outreach to patients in the community?
questions.explanation: Assertive community treatment is based on the model whereby teams of psychiatrists and other mental health workers go out into the community to patients' homes to maintain contact with them, monitor their status, and encourage medication compliance. The goal is to prevent decompensation of severely mentally ill patients and catch them before they severely decompensate and require hospitalization.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents to your office complaining of long-standing lower extremity discomfort, particularly at night before sleep onset. She reports shooting pains in the lower extremities that are relieved upon standing or walking. The discomfort is described as a 'crawling' sensation. The treatment of choice for her condition is:
questions.explanation: The condition described is restless legs syndrome (RLS). One of the most common treatments is ropinirole (Requip), a dopamine agonist, which can improve symptoms at low doses starting at 0.5 mg before bedtime. Other dopamine agonists (pergolide, pramipexole, bromocriptine) can be useful as well, along with benzodiazepines, opiate analgesics, gabapentin, and levodopa-carbidopa. It is usually idiopathic but has been associated with polyneuropathy, uremia, and iron deficiency. Classic symptoms are crawling or creeping sensations of the lower extremities worse when lying down or in bed, occurring most often at sleep onset; urge to move the legs relieved by movement; symptoms worse at night. Family history positive in 40-50% of patients, suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance. Suvorexant (Belsomra) is a sleep medication not indicated for RLS; it works via orexin receptor antagonism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best diagnostic procedure to determine if a 12-year-old boy is depressed?

options.text: Interview the child's teacher by phone

questions.explanation: The best method to diagnose depression is the standard psychiatric interview. Psychiatric interviews serve two functions: to find and classify symptoms and to find psychological determinants of behavior. Interviews can be insight- or symptom-oriented. The other answer choices all have major flaws. The MMPI is a self-report inventory used to assess personality traits and is not appropriate to the task. The scholastic achievement test is completely unrelated to symptom identification for depression. The dexamethasone suppression test demonstrates abnormal HPA axis activity found in 50% of major depression patients but has limited clinical usefulness due to frequent false-positive and false-negative results. Interviewing the patient's teacher is a good idea but cannot replace a face-to-face meeting with the child or be the sole basis for diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency room with acute onset of vertigo, nausea, vomiting, dysarthria, and nystagmus. On further examination, he is noted to have loss of pain and temperature sensation to the left-hand side of his face. He has right-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation to his trunk and leg. He has a left Horner's syndrome and falls to his left-hand side when you ask him to walk, and he has left finger-to-nose dysmetria. You diagnose an acute stroke, which is most likely localized to the:
questions.explanation: This question describes a left lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg's syndrome), a brainstem stroke syndrome usually caused by occlusion of one of the vertebral arteries or, less commonly, one of the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries. The area of infarction is the lateral medulla. The clinical syndrome involves ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the face, cerebellar ataxia, and weakness of the vocal cords, pharynx, and palate, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation to the body. The visual system is not affected in this syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is associated with violence and aggression?

options.text: Blunted response to corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation test
Blunted growth hormone response to hypoglycemia
Increased levels of norepinephrine in the CSF

questions.explanation: Decreased levels of serotonin in the CSF have been shown to be linked to higher levels of aggression in patients. In general, dopamine seems to promote aggression, whereas NE and serotonin seem to inhibit it, as does GABA. Rapid declines in serotonin levels have been linked to irritability and aggression, and low CSF serotonin has been linked to increased frequency of suicide. CRH is a hormone that may increase in major depression, anorexia, and anxiety disorders (produced by the hypothalamus) but has no relation to aggression. Growth hormone is also unrelated to aggression.

questions.question_text: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is inherited by an _____ pattern of inheritance and results in a deficiency in _____:
questions.explanation: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder of myelin resulting in deficiency of arylsulfatase A (ASA), causing abnormal accumulation of sulfatides in the brain and peripheral nerves and progressive demyelination. The ASA gene is on chromosome 22q13. Gait disorder with hypotonia and lower-limb areflexia are early manifestations that often precede CNS involvement in infantile/juvenile forms; adult-onset MLD presents with progressive dementia and behavioral problems. Nerve conduction velocities are slowed in juvenile and adult patients; delayed visual and somatosensory-evoked potential latencies are noted more in adult cases. Classic neuropathologic findings are segmental nerve demyelination and metachromatic inclusions within Schwann cells and macrophages. MRI combined with urine sulfatide assay and ASA enzyme assay in leukocytes is the preferred, less invasive diagnostic method. Bone marrow transplantation may slow or stop disease progression. Tay-Sachs disease (autosomal recessive gangliosidosis, hexosaminidase A deficiency, chromosome 15q23-q24) presents with developmental retardation, paralysis, dementia, blindness, death by age 2-3, cherry-red spot, hypersensitivity to loud noise. Krabbe's disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy, autosomal recessive, galactocerebrosidase β-galactosidase deficiency, chromosome 14q31) presents with multinucleated macrophages in central white matter, rapid deterioration, hypertonicity, optic atrophy, opisthotonic posture, seizures; stem cell transplantation can improve CNS manifestations.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not true with respect to seasonal affective disorder (SAD)?

options.text: Patients are likely to respond well to light therapy
The 'with seasonal pattern' specifier can be applied to bipolar I, bipolar II, and major depressive disorders according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)
It is not necessary to have full remission of symptoms at other times of the year to make this diagnosis
SAD involves a regular temporal relationship between the onset of symptoms and the time of year
The physician must demonstrate at least two depressive episodes at the same time of year to make the diagnosis

correct_answer.text: It is not necessary to have full remission of symptoms at other times of the year to make this diagnosis

correct_answers.text: It is not necessary to have full remission of symptoms at other times of the year to make this diagnosis

questions.explanation: SAD is a non-DSM term used to describe a seasonal pattern specifier added to the diagnoses of bipolar I and II disorders and major depressive disorder. It is associated with depressive symptoms occurring at a certain time of year and complete remission at other times. One must show a pattern of two episodes during the same season over the previous 2 years to make the diagnosis, and the seasonal depressive episodes must substantially outnumber any non-seasonally related depressive episodes during the patient's lifetime. The treatment is light therapy. Seasonal affective disorder is often associated with carbohydrate cravings, light therapy is most effective in the morning, and light therapy can precipitate hypomania in bipolar patients.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following primitive reflexes is not generally expected to disappear by about 6 months of age?
questions.explanation: The parachute response can persist longer than 6 months. The Moro reflex is elicited by startle and is usually present in the normal infant up to 6 months of age; the child extends the arms symmetrically when the head is rapidly but gently dropped a few centimeters with the baby supine. The tonic neck reflex is normally present from birth to about 3 months. Grasp and rooting reflexes usually disappear at or about the 6-month age mark; persistence beyond this period or recurrence later in life is abnormal. Positive grasp and rooting reflexes in the adult are considered frontal release signs, signaling extensive frontal white matter damage or disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would fall under the heading of 'Other Specified Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders'?

options.text: A patient with pain in one or more areas that is thought to be significantly mediated by psychological factors
A patient with a persistent belief that he or she has cancer despite reassurance by his or her physician that nothing is wrong
A patient who develops a motor deficit following significant psychological stressors
A patient who feels that she is pregnant and presents with amenorrhea, enlarged abdomen, and breast engorgement but a negative pregnancy test
A patient who has medical complaints involving pain, gastrointestinal complaints, neurological complaints, and sexual complaints, but no medical explanation can be found for these symptoms

correct_answer.text: A patient who feels that she is pregnant and presents with amenorrhea, enlarged abdomen, and breast engorgement but a negative pregnancy test

correct_answers.text: A patient who feels that she is pregnant and presents with amenorrhea, enlarged abdomen, and breast engorgement but a negative pregnancy test

questions.explanation: Answer choice D describes pseudocyesis, listed in the DSM under 'Other Specified Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders.' It involves a false belief that one is pregnant, potentially with physical signs of pregnancy, but the patient is not pregnant and there is no endocrine disorder to explain the findings. Choice A describes somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain (pain not explained by medical condition, mediated by psychological factors). Choice B describes illness anxiety disorder (conviction of serious disease despite reassurance). Choice C describes conversion disorder/functional neurological symptom disorder (neurologic symptoms with no medical explanation, mediated by psychological factors). Choice E describes somatic symptom disorder (somatic complaints with no medical explanation, associated with psychological factors, requiring excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors about the symptoms).

questions.question_text: An AIDS patient presents with decreased visual acuity. The most likely offending infectious agent responsible for this presentation is:
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus is the most common offending infectious agent in AIDS-related retinopathy, accounting for 30% of cases of HIV-related retinopathy. Toxoplasmosis is less common (about 5% of retinitis cases). Tuberculosis is a rare cause of AIDS-related retinitis. Cryptococcus neoformans is usually responsible for fungal meningitis, not retinitis, in AIDS patients with low CD4 counts. JC virus is the offending agent in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in AIDS patients.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not true regarding schizophrenia?

options.text: The disorder is chronic and usually has a prodromal phase
Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia
The patient's overall functioning declines or fails to reach the expected level
The most frequent hallucinations are olfactory
Social withdrawal and emotional disengagement are common

correct_answer.text: The most frequent hallucinations are olfactory

correct_answers.text: The most frequent hallucinations are olfactory

questions.explanation: The most common hallucinations in schizophrenia are auditory. Visual, olfactory, and tactile hallucinations are also possible. Schizophrenia was first discovered by Morel, who called it 'démence precoce.' Later Kraepelin used 'dementia praecox' to describe a group of illnesses that started in adolescence and ended in dementia. Bleuler coined the term 'schizophrenia.' The disorder is chronic and has a prodromal, active, and residual phase.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not seen in narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: Nighttime awakening is not considered part of the clinical picture of narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is a lifelong sleep disorder with a hereditary component; US prevalence is about 3 to 6 in 10,000. Narcolepsy is linked to dysfunction of the hypocretin (orexin) peptide system. The hallmark is excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep attacks (irresistible desire to fall asleep, lasting a few minutes to 30 minutes). The second major manifestation is cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone in voluntary muscles, respiratory/ocular muscles spared, consciousness preserved; occurs in 60-100% of narcoleptic patients). Sleep paralysis (hypnagogic/hypnopompic bilateral or unilateral limb paralysis with preserved consciousness) occurs in one-quarter to one-half of patients. Hypnagogic hallucinations occur in about 20-40% of patients. Other symptoms include disturbance of night sleep (70-80%) and automatic behavior (20-40%). Medications include modafinil, armodafinil (Nuvigil), and sodium oxybate (Xyrem); combination of modafinil and Xyrem is often most effective.

questions.question_text: Uncontrollable excessive talking, as seen in mania, is also known as:
questions.explanation: Logorrhea is uncontrollable, excessive talking. Alexithymia is a difficulty in recognizing and describing one's emotions. Echolalia is the imitative repetition of the speech of another. Flight of ideas is rapid shifting from one topic to another. Stilted speech is a formal, stiff speech pattern.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not an appropriate therapy for status epilepticus?

options.text: Oxygen by nasal cannula with airway protection

questions.explanation: Intramuscular phenytoin is a poor choice for treatment of status epilepticus because of its erratic rate of absorption. Useful status epilepticus treatments include rectal or intravenous diazepam, intravenous lorazepam, intravenous phenytoin or fosphenytoin, intravenous valproic acid, oxygen by nasal cannula and airway protection, and intravenous phenobarbital. Phenobarbital is acceptable but not the best choice because of the narrow therapeutic window and possibility of overdose leading to respiratory depression and possible death.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding atypical antipsychotics?

options.text: Ziprasidone is an agonist at the serotonin (5-HT) 1A receptor and an inhibitor of reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine
Risperidone is a significantly weaker antagonist of the dopamine D2 receptor than haloperidol
Quetiapine is known for its high incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms
Olanzapine has been associated with weight loss in the majority of patients
Clozapine has been shown to increase suicidality in chronically ill patients

correct_answer.text: Ziprasidone is an agonist at the serotonin (5-HT) 1A receptor and an inhibitor of reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine

correct_answers.text: Ziprasidone is an agonist at the serotonin (5-HT) 1A receptor and an inhibitor of reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine

questions.explanation: Of the statements listed, the only correct one is answer choice A. Ziprasidone is an agonist at 5-HT 1A and does inhibit reuptake of serotonin and NE. It is also an antagonist at 5-HT 1D, 2A, and 2C, as well as dopamine D2 and D3, with low affinity for histaminic, muscarinic, and α2 receptors; because of its serotonin/NE action, it has been postulated to benefit anxiety and depression as well as psychosis. Risperidone is a similar D2 blocker to haldol and carries one of the highest EPS risks among atypicals. Quetiapine has low EPS incidence (only moderate D2 affinity), high affinity for 5-HT 2/6, H1, α1/α2, low muscarinic affinity. Olanzapine is associated with weight gain and is very anticholinergic. Clozapine is associated with decreased suicide risk in schizophrenic patients; major side effects include seizures and agranulocytosis. The treatment of choice for anticholinergic urinary retention is Urecholine (bethanechol).

questions.question_text: Which of the following anticonvulsant agents is most appropriate for primary generalized seizures, including tonic–clonic, absence, atonic, and myoclonic seizure types?
questions.explanation: Divalproex sodium (valproic acid) has the broadest spectrum of coverage and indication of all the anticonvulsant medications, with proven efficacy in primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, and myoclonic seizures. Its mechanism is blockade of voltage-dependent sodium channels and GABA enhancement. Phenytoin is not indicated for absence seizures (indicated for partial and generalized tonic-clonic seizures; blocks voltage-dependent sodium channels). Oxcarbazepine and carbamazepine are indicated for partial complex and secondary generalized seizures but can worsen absence seizures; oxcarbazepine does not autoinduce its own metabolism the way carbamazepine does. Ethosuximide is indicated only for uncomplicated absence seizures (lowers voltage-dependent calcium conductance in thalamic neurons). Valbenazine (Ingrezza) is indicated for tardive dyskinesia, inhibiting VMAT2; not used for seizures.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a side effect of the tricyclic antidepressants?
questions.explanation: Constipation is a common side effect of the tricyclic antidepressants as a result of the anticholinergic activity of these drugs. Other tricyclic side effects include dry mouth, blurry vision, sweating, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, lethargy, agitation, tremor, slowed cardiac conduction (prolonged PR and QRS intervals), and tachycardia.

questions.question_text: The L5 motor nerve root innervates the nerves responsible for:
questions.explanation: Foot flexion (dorsiflexion; bending of the foot upward) involves the tibialis anterior muscle innervated by nerves from the L5 motor nerve root; L5 also controls extension of the big toe (extensor hallucis longus). A lesion at L5 often causes foot drop from dorsiflexor weakness. Foot extension (pushing down on the gas pedal) involves the gastrocnemius/soleus, innervated predominantly by S1. Leg extension is a function of the quadriceps (L3/L4). Hip flexion is a function of the iliopsoas muscles (L1, L2, L3). The Achilles/ankle jerk reflex is a function of the S1 motor nerve root.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following antidepressants can be used as an antipruritic agent and for the treatment of gastric ulcer because of its potent histamine blockade?
questions.explanation: Amitriptyline can be used for gastric ulcer because of its strong histamine blockade. Other drugs that can also be used for this purpose include doxepin and trimipramine. Vilazodone (Viibryd), a serotonin modulator indicated for major depression, is unrelated to gastric ulcer; it works by inhibiting serotonin reuptake and partially agonizing the 5HT 1A receptor.

questions.question_text: A patient involved in a car accident is found on MRI to have a spinal fracture and a partial crush lesion to the cervical spinal cord that effectively causes a functional hemisection of the cord. His deficits would be expected to include:

options.text: Contralateral loss of motor control and pain and temperature sensation with ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
Ipsilateral loss of motor control and pain and temperature sensation with contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation
Ipsilateral loss of motor control and proprioception and vibration sensation with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
Contralateral loss of motor control and proprioception and vibration sensation with ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation
Ipsilateral loss of motor control and contralateral loss of proprioception, vibration, pain, and temperature sensation

correct_answer.text: Ipsilateral loss of motor control and proprioception and vibration sensation with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation

correct_answers.text: Ipsilateral loss of motor control and proprioception and vibration sensation with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation

questions.explanation: The condition noted is the classic Brown-Séquard syndrome due to a hemisection of the spinal cord. The correct combination of deficits is loss of motor control and posterior column function ipsilateral to and below the level of the lesion, coupled with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation one to two dermatomal levels below the level of the lesion. Frequent causes include disk herniation, penetrating trauma, spinal fracture, and radiation injury. The cervical spinal cord is most commonly affected.

questions.question_text: A child is able to use some symbols and language. Her reasoning is intuitive. She is unable to think logically or deductively. Which of Piaget's stages does this child fit into?
questions.explanation: This question focuses on Piaget's stages of cognitive development. In the sensorimotor stage, children respond to stimuli in the environment, learning during the process, eventually developing object permanence and beginning to understand symbols. During the preoperational stage, there is a sense that punishment for bad deeds is unavoidable (immanent justice), a sense of egocentrism and phenomenalistic causality, and animistic thinking. In the concrete operations stage, egocentric thought changes to operational thought; children can order and group objects, and develop understanding of conservation and reversibility. During formal operations children can think abstractly, reason deductively, and define abstract concepts. Trust vs mistrust is one of Erik Erikson's stages and is a distractor in this question.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old man suffers a stroke with loss of motor functioning in the left leg and, to a lesser extent, the left arm. He has abulia, and his eyes and head seem preferentially deviated to the right. His left arm is apraxic. His head CT is shown. The arterial territory involved is that of the:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) territory is the area affected by this stroke. The ACA irrigates the medial frontal lobes; therefore when affected it causes preferential leg greater than arm and face weakness contralateral to the side of the lesion. Destruction of the nearby frontal eye fields causes loss of tonic opposition of gaze to the opposite side, so the eyes often look toward the side of the lesion. Sphincteric incontinence is sometimes seen if cortical bowel and bladder areas are affected. Patients often suffer from abulia (loss of will power/lack of ability to do things independently). Bilateral ACA territory damage can result in akinetic mutism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding norepinephrine (NE) and/or the locus ceruleus?

options.text: NE is synthesized in the locus ceruleus
Dopamine is synthesized in the locus ceruleus, NE in the dorsal raphe nuclei
Acetylcholine is synthesized with NE in the substantia nigra
5-HT is synthesized in the locus ceruleus
The locus ceruleus is the site of the formation of serotonin

correct_answer.text: NE is synthesized in the locus ceruleus

correct_answers.text: NE is synthesized in the locus ceruleus

questions.explanation: NE is made in the locus ceruleus. Serotonin is made in the dorsal raphe nuclei. Dopamine is made in the substantia nigra. Acetylcholine is made in the nucleus basalis of Meynert.

questions.question_text: Pure motor hemiparesis is most likely to result from a stroke localized to the:
questions.explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis is one of the classic lacunar stroke syndromes and would be expected from an infarct in the area of the internal capsule, the basis pontis, or the corona radiata. Lacunar strokes are ischemic strokes resulting from small-vessel lipohyalinosis, for which hypertension and diabetes are the two major risk factors. Lacunar infarcts are small, ranging from 0.5 mm to 1.5 cm in diameter; microembolism may also be a mechanism. Other lacunar syndromes include pure sensory stroke (small lesion in ventroposterolateral thalamic nucleus); sensorimotor stroke (internal capsule and thalamus or posterior limb of internal capsule); ataxic hemiparesis (basis pontis or posterior limb of internal capsule); and dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome (deep areas of the basis pontis).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following receptor types is associated with weight gain and sedation?
questions.explanation: Of the receptors listed, it is the histamine receptor that is associated with weight gain and sedation. The M1 receptor is associated with constipation, blurred vision, dry mouth, and drowsiness. The α1 receptors are associated with dizziness and decreased blood pressure. The 5-HT 1A receptor is a presynaptic autoreceptor involved in the response of neurons to SSRIs. The 5-HT 2A receptor is one of the postsynaptic serotonin receptors involved in the response to SSRIs. The serotonin receptors are associated with modulation of depression and anxiety but not with weight gain or sedation.

questions.question_text: The lesion causing a left-arm hemiballismus would most likely localize to the:
questions.explanation: The contralateral subthalamic nucleus of Luys is most often the area where a lesion will produce hemiballismus. Hemiballismus is a dramatic, flinging movement of the proximal extremities. It can affect both upper and lower limbs and is most often unilateral. Most frequently, the cause of hemiballismus is an acute stroke.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a biogenic amine neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: The six biogenic amine neurotransmitters are dopamine, epinephrine, NE, acetylcholine, histamine, and serotonin. Of these, dopamine, NE, and epinephrine are all synthesized from the precursor tyrosine and are known as a group as the catecholamines. GABA is an amino acid neurotransmitter, not a biogenic amine. Cocaine works by blocking the reuptake of the biogenic amines, more specifically serotonin, NE, and dopamine.

questions.question_text: The mechanism of action by which reserpine both improves the symptoms of adult-onset primary focal dystonia and can cause depression is:
questions.explanation: Reserpine interferes with the magnesium and ATP-dependent uptake of biogenic amines, which results in the depletion of dopamine, NE, and serotonin neurotransmitters. In this way, it can relieve symptoms of dystonia and can also cause depression, sedation, and a Parkinson's-like syndrome.

questions.question_text: In the psychotic patient, the defense mechanism of projection takes the form of:
questions.explanation: Projection is perceiving and reacting to unacceptable inner impulses as though they were outside the self. On a psychotic level, it takes the form of delusions about external realities that are usually persecutory in nature. A patient's own impulses and hostilities are projected onto another, who is now assumed to have intentions to persecute the patient. The other answer choices are distractors that have nothing to do with projection.

questions.question_text: The drainage of CSF into the blood is a function of the:
questions.explanation: The arachnoid granulations are the major sites for drainage of CSF into the blood, protruding through the dura into the superior sagittal sinus and acting as one-way valves or siphons. Equilibrium is maintained by the arachnoid granulations; if CSF pressure drops below a certain level, absorption stops, and if pressure increases, more fluid is absorbed. The choroid plexuses that protrude into the ventricles are responsible for the majority of CSF production in humans (rate about 0.35 mL/min). Drugs that can temporarily reduce CSF production and ease increased intracranial pressure include acetazolamide and mannitol. States of hypothermia, hypocarbia, hypoxia, and hyperosmolality can also temporarily decrease CSF production. Virchow-Robin spaces act as a duct for substances in the subarachnoid space to enter the brain.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a method of making a prediction to compare the value of one variable to another?
questions.explanation: Regression analysis is a method of predicting the value of one variable in relation to another variable based on observed data. Probability is the likelihood that an event will occur (0 = will not occur, 1 = will definitely occur). Point prevalence is the number of people with a disorder at a specific point in time divided by the total population at that point in time. Incidence is the number of new cases of a disease over a given time divided by the total number of people at risk during that time. Central tendency is a central value in a distribution around which other values are arranged (mean, median, mode). Kappa is a variable used to indicate a constant value that does not change. Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect that which is being tested for.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old woman with a history of smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and myocardial infarction presents to your emergency room by ambulance with an acute onset of obtundation with dense right hemiplegia; right hemisensory loss to light touch, pain, and temperature; and mutism. You suspect a left lobar hemorrhage because of the acuteness of onset of her symptoms and a blood pressure reading of 210/100 mm Hg in the emergency room. Once stabilized, the best immediate diagnostic test of choice from the emergency room would be:

options.text: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure and CSF assay for xanthochromia
Blood work for coagulation panel (PT, PTT [partial thromboplastin time], INR [international normalized ratio])

questions.explanation: Noncontrast head CT is the best immediate test of choice in the emergency room if a lobar hemorrhage is suspected. MRI can add precision but may not reveal acute bleeding as well as CT in the hyperacute stage. The most common location of intracranial hemorrhage is the putamen (about 35% of cases); lobar hemorrhage accounts for about one-quarter of cases. Hypertension is the most frequent cause of intracranial hemorrhage, but AVMs, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and sympathomimetic agents also contribute. ER management begins with stabilization of vital signs and airway protection; intubation is indicated if GCS drops to 8 or less. CT scan of the head must be done next; neurosurgical consultation may be indicated if hemorrhage is large. Coagulation panel checking is very important; reversal of anticoagulation with protamine sulfate (heparin) or vitamin K/FFP (warfarin) as needed. Bedside EEG is not indicated unless pervasive coma or seizures. Lumbar puncture is usually contraindicated if intracranial or lobar hemorrhage is suspected due to risk of uncal herniation; LP with CSF xanthochromia assay is useful only if subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is most closely associated with prognostic outcome in psychodynamic therapy?
questions.explanation: Outcomes in psychodynamic therapy have been found to be closely associated with the empathy provided by the therapist. The goal is for the therapist to be in tune with the patient's internal state in an empathetic way. When patients feel that therapists understand their internal world, they are more likely to accept interpretations made by the therapist. The other answer choices, although important, are not the most important; some distractors may affect the therapeutic relationship but will not universally be the most important factor in the outcome of therapy.

questions.question_text: Melatonin is a neuronal hormone that promotes sleep and is produced in the brain by the:
questions.explanation: Melatonin is believed to be released principally by the pineal gland, and there is a feedback loop between the pineal gland and the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus that helps with sleep regulation. Melatonin is secreted predominantly at night, with levels peaking between 3:00 am and 5:00 am and decreasing to lower levels during the day. Melatonin is a modulator of human circadian rhythm for entrainment by the light-dark cycle.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an objective psychological test?
questions.explanation: The MMPI is an objective psychological test, a self-report inventory used to find areas of pathological personality structure. The other tests listed are projective tests, in which the patient is given a picture or incomplete piece of information and asked to fill in the details or complete the unfinished task, revealing aspects of personality, thought content, thought structure, and psychological makeup. In the Rorschach test, the patient is shown ink blots and asked to share what he or she thinks they look like. In the sentence completion test, the patient finishes incomplete sentences. In the thematic apperception test, the patient is shown pictures and makes up stories. In the draw-a-person test, the patient draws persons of the same and opposite sex, with the same-sex figure thought to represent the patient; interpretations are made based on the details of the drawings.

questions.question_text: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare late complication of which one of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is the result of a persistent and nonproductive viral infection of the neurons and glia caused by the measles virus, a late complication of measles. Children 5 to 10 years of age are affected most often. Clinical manifestations include personality and cognitive changes, myoclonic seizures, spasticity, choreoathetoid movements, and difficulty swallowing, eventually leading to coma and death. The three tests of choice are lumbar puncture for CSF assay, EEG, and brain biopsy. CSF reveals elevated measles antibody titer, oligoclonal bands, absence of pleocytosis, normal glucose, and normal-to-elevated protein. Brain biopsy may reveal neuronal and glial nuclear and cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies. EEG reveals periodic bursts of generalized slow-wave complexes. There is no specific accepted treatment, but intraventricular interferon-α combined with oral isoprinosine can be helpful. Prognosis is generally poor. There is no evidence that SSPE results from measles vaccination in children.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following does not describe a patient with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?

options.text: The patient fails to follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork
The patient often fidgets with hands or feet or squirms in his or her seat
The patient often has difficulty awaiting his or her turn
The patient often seems not to listen when spoken to directly
The patient shows impairment from symptoms at school but not at home

correct_answer.text: The patient shows impairment from symptoms at school but not at home

correct_answers.text: The patient shows impairment from symptoms at school but not at home

questions.explanation: ADHD is diagnosed by six or more symptoms of inattention or six or more symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity that persist for 6 months or more. Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms should be present before age 12, and symptoms of impairment must be present in more than one setting. Symptoms of inattention involve failure to pay close attention, failure to sustain attention, not listening, not following through, problems organizing tasks, forgetfulness, and being easily distracted. Symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity include fidgeting, inability to remain seated, running or climbing excessively, difficulty playing quietly, acting as if driven by a motor, talking excessively, blurting out answers, difficulty awaiting turn, and interrupting others.

questions.question_text: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room from a group home because of acute agitation. On examination you note choreoathetotic movements, hyperreflexia, acute agitation, self-scratching and mutilating behavior, and marked cognitive impairment. You peruse the group-home chart and note that this young boy has an enzymatic deficiency in hypoxanthine–guanine phosphoribosyltransferase. Your keen memory brings you back to your pediatrics rotation in medical school, and you realize the diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive hereditary disorder of purine and pyrimidine metabolism. Hyperuricemia results from a deficiency in hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase. Clinical symptoms include choreoathetosis, hyperreflexia, hypertonia, dysarthria, behavioral disturbances, cognitive impairment, and self-mutilatory behavior, probably resulting from diminished dopamine concentrations in the CSF and basal ganglia. Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, localizing to chromosome 22. Tay-Sachs is a recessive disorder localizing to chromosome 15, caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency; the adult form presents as progressive proximal weakness with spasticity, dysarthria, and cognitive/psychiatric impairment. Krabbe's disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) is autosomal recessive, localizing to chromosome 14, caused by galactocerebroside β-galactosidase deficiency, with generalized demyelination, globoid cells, and infantile arrest of motor/cognitive development. Gaucher's disease is autosomal recessive, resulting from β-glucosidase deficiency, localizing to chromosome 1; Type I presents with hematologic anomalies, hypersplenism, bone lesions, skin pigmentation, and ocular pingueculae.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a DSM criterion for schizophrenia?

options.text: Presence of active-phase symptoms for 6 months

correct_answer.text: Presence of active-phase symptoms for 6 months

correct_answers.text: Presence of active-phase symptoms for 6 months

questions.explanation: To diagnose schizophrenia, active-phase symptoms must be present for a 1-month period only. It may be diagnosed if other symptoms (i.e., negative) are present over a 6-month period, but active-phase symptoms must be present for at least 1 month of those 6 months. All other answer choices are part of the characteristic active-phase symptoms for schizophrenia. Social isolation is a bad prognostic sign for schizophrenia. Good prognostic signs include late age of onset, acute onset, and the presence of an affective component.

questions.question_text: Botulinum toxin type A is not the treatment of choice for which one of the following disorders?

options.text: Limb spasticity related to multiple sclerosis

questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin type A is FDA-approved for the treatment of cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm, strabismus, and axillary hyperhidrosis, and it's approved cosmetically for hyperactive glabellar lines of the procerus muscles of the forehead. Although not FDA-approved for spasticity related to multiple sclerosis, it is an excellent treatment for that particular disorder. Botulinum toxin type A is also used off-label for the treatment of migraine. The mechanism of action is through blockade of neuromuscular transmission via blockade of presynaptic acetylcholine release. Botulinum toxin type A has no place in the treatment of RLS.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with a delusion about being poisoned that has been present for 5 months. The patient has no hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms. There has been no major effect on the patient's daily functioning. The patient has no mood symptoms. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: This question is a clear description of a delusional disorder. In a delusional disorder, the patient usually presents with a bizarre or nonbizarre delusion. There are no other psychotic symptoms present. His ability to function in his daily life is preserved. There is not a significant mood component to the disease. The question says nothing about memory impairment; therefore dementia is not correct. The patient does not meet criteria for active-phase schizophrenic symptoms; therefore schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder are ruled out. Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than a month, and this patient has had symptoms for 5 months, so this answer choice is incorrect.

questions.question_text: A young woman presents to the emergency room with a complaint of a band-like, bifrontal, squeezing headache that began 6 hours earlier. She denies nausea, vomiting, or any other associated symptoms. She describes the pain as waxing and waning in intensity throughout the 6-hour period. Physical examination is unremarkable. She reports suffering from similar attacks in the past. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is that of classic tension-type or muscle-contraction headache, resulting from both muscular and emotional tension and stress; the pathogenesis is not well understood. Treatment with rest, sleep, or simple analgesics is often sufficient; headaches can begin at any age, are most often bilateral, described as band-like, squeezing/pressure/burning pain, can wax and wane over hours to days, and are usually free of associated or autonomic symptoms, differentiating from migraine. Treatment usually begins with aspirin or acetaminophen; combination drugs like Fioricet or NSAIDs may help for more severe headaches. Migraine is differentiated mainly by stereotyped features and autonomic symptoms (unilateral, pulsatile, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, nausea/vomiting, anorexia, blurred vision, light-headedness). Aura involves transient visual, motor, or focal neurologic symptoms; scintillating scotoma is the most common visual aura manifestation; sensory aura involves transient numbness/tingling; motor aura is rare and can be mistaken for stroke. Basilar migraine presents with occipital headache and brainstem symptoms (vertigo, dysarthria, tinnitus, speech deficits), possibly with loss of consciousness. Paroxysmal hemicrania is an indomethacin-responsive headache syndrome, more common in women, with frequent brief unilateral attacks accompanied by autonomic features (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, ptosis, rhinorrhea) and dramatic response to indomethacin.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not consistent with a major depressive episode?
questions.explanation: In major depressive disorder, libido is decreased. Increased libido is often found in mania.

questions.question_text: Sophie has been seeing her primary care physician due to hirsutism, obesity, and the recent diagnosis of type II diabetes. Her doctor has now diagnosed her with polycystic ovarian syndrome. Based on this new diagnosis, which psychiatric comorbidity is she most likely to experience?
questions.explanation: Generally speaking there is a higher prevalence of psychiatric disorders in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome than in the general population. The disorder with the most elevated rates in polycystic ovarian syndrome is depression, found to be the most significantly increased psychiatric condition in several studies. Depakote (used frequently in bipolar disorder) is known to cause polycystic ovarian syndrome, leading to hair loss, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and metabolic syndrome.

questions.question_text: A patient comes to your clinic with complaint of hypersomnia, hyperphagia, psychomotor slowing, and depressed mood. He states that this happens yearly, usually around October or November. The treatment plan for this man should include:

options.text: Exposure to bright artificial light for 2 to 6 hours per day.

correct_answer.text: Exposure to bright artificial light for 2 to 6 hours per day.

correct_answers.text: Exposure to bright artificial light for 2 to 6 hours per day.

questions.explanation: This is a case of SAD, a depression that sets in during the fall and winter and resolves during the spring and summer. It is often characterized by hypersomnia, hyperphagia, and psychomotor slowing. Treatment involves exposure to bright artificial light for 2 to 6 hours each day during the fall and winter months. It is thought to be related to abnormal melatonin metabolism. All other answer choices given are distractors and are unrelated to the patient's primary problem.

questions.question_text: What is the mechanism of action of carbidopa in the combination agent carbidopa–levodopa that is used for the treatment of Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa serves a simple function: it inhibits DOPA decarboxylase and thereby prevents the peripheral metabolism of levodopa to dopamine before it can cross the blood-brain barrier. Dopamine agonists such as ropinirole, pramipexole, pergolide, and bromocriptine are direct postsynaptic dopamine receptor agonists indicated for Parkinson's disease treatment. Selegiline is the selective MAO-B inhibitor that blocks dopamine degradation by MAO-B and can potentiate the action of levodopa in the CNS. COMT inhibitors (tolcapone, entacapone) prevent peripheral degradation of levodopa and central metabolism of levodopa/dopamine, thereby increasing central levels; usually taken simultaneously with levodopa-carbidopa. Anticholinergic agents (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) reduce tremor by blockade of postsynaptic muscarinic receptors, carrying risks of confusion, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and dry mouth.

questions.question_text: A young woman presents to the emergency room with complaints of palpitations, sweating, shortness of breath, chest pain, and nausea. She thinks that she is having a heart attack. Electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals normal sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. Cardiac enzymes are not elevated. Given her symptoms, an alternative diagnosis would be:
questions.explanation: This question includes common symptoms found in a panic attack. Others include trembling, choking sensations, dizziness, fear of losing control, fear of death, paresthesias, chills, or hot flushes. Lifetime prevalence of panic disorder is 1% to 4%. The patient in question does not present with the characteristic signs and symptoms of a manic episode. Myxedema madness is a depressed and psychotic state found in some patients with hypothyroidism. Mad Hatter syndrome presents as manic symptoms resulting from chronic mercury intoxication. The patient describes no psychotic symptoms, so psychotic disorder NOS is clearly the wrong choice. The organic differential for panic disorder includes hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, irritable bowel syndrome, migraines, angina, asthma, epilepsy, Huntington's disease, hyperparathyroidism, amphetamine intoxication, cocaine, marijuana, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol withdrawal, mitral valve prolapse, and B12 deficiency.

questions.question_text: The phenomenon of apoptosis refers to:
questions.explanation: Apoptosis refers to programmed neuronal cell death. This concept is believed to account for the pathophysiology of several neurodegenerative diseases, including spinal muscular atrophy, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Alzheimer's dementia.

questions.question_text: You are reviewing previous treatment records for a new patient that you are about to meet for the first time. You note that they carry a diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder. Based on this information, which defense mechanism is this patient most likely to exhibit?
questions.explanation: People with paranoid personality disorder externalize their own emotions and use the defense of projection. They attribute to others the impulses and thoughts they cannot accept in themselves. They are characterized by long-standing suspiciousness and mistrust of others. Other defense mechanisms are discussed elsewhere in this volume.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old toddler is brought to the emergency room because of seizures, hemiparesis, and apparent blindness. You immediately notice a marked reddish discoloration of the left side of the forehead and face. The parents tell you that their child has not met appropriate developmental milestones. Your most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder that is sporadic and not genetically inherited. The hallmark is the presence of a facial cutaneous angioma (port-wine nevus), usually with a brain angioma ipsilateral to the skin lesion. Other characteristics can include contralateral hemiparesis, mental retardation, and homonymous hemianopia. Glaucoma is common and if untreated can lead to blindness. Seizures develop in over 70% of Sturge-Weber patients and present most often as motor seizures or generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Treatment of seizures is achieved with anticonvulsant medication, which if ineffective may lead to surgical intervention such as hemispherectomy. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL) is heritable, autosomal dominant, with a tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 3, characterized by retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas (most commonly cerebellum), visceral cysts/tumors, renal cysts, and pheochromocytoma. Ataxia-telangiectasia is a neurodegenerative disorder, autosomal recessive, with early-onset ataxia developing around 12 months, telangiectases developing from age 3-6 years, and higher risk of lymphoma/leukemia, along with abnormal eye movements. Fabry's disease is X-linked, caused by α-galactosidase A deficiency, with red/purple papules, corneal deposits, painful dysesthesias, cerebral thrombosis/hemorrhage, and renal failure (renal transplantation can delay but not cure). Tuberous sclerosis is discussed elsewhere.

questions.question_text: How is a doctor who agrees to take Medicare paid?

options.text: He or she agrees to take only what Medicare pays for the service
He or she is allowed to bill the patient for the difference between what Medicare pays and what he or she charges
He or she is paid by a third party to make up the difference between the fee-for-service rate and the fee allowed by Medicare
He or she can sue the government if the full fee is not paid
He or she is not allowed to charge copays

correct_answer.text: He or she agrees to take only what Medicare pays for the service

correct_answers.text: He or she agrees to take only what Medicare pays for the service

questions.explanation: The doctor who takes Medicare must accept Medicare's maximum fee. This fee includes any appropriate co-pays set forth in the patient's policy. The physician cannot bill the patient or another party for the difference between what Medicare allows and what the physician wants to charge.

questions.question_text: The pain syndrome known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy does not involve which one of the following characteristics?

options.text: Warm or hot skin on the extremities

correct_answer.text: Warm or hot skin on the extremities

correct_answers.text: Warm or hot skin on the extremities

questions.explanation: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy is one of the so-called complex regional pain syndromes, resulting from regional pain and sensory changes after trauma or a noxious event; there may or may not be a diagnosable underlying nerve lesion. Soft tissue injury is the trigger in about 40% of cases, and bony fracture in about 25%. There are three stages: Stage 1 (acute) with pain out of proportion to the initial injury and hypersensitivity; Stage 2 (dystrophic) with tissue edema and skin that is cool, cyanotic, hyperhidrotic, with livedo reticularis, constant pain increasing with contact; Stage 3 (atrophic) with paroxysmal pain and irreversible tissue damage, thin/shiny skin, thickened/contractured fascia. Treatments begin with intense physical therapy; steroids may help in certain cases; phenoxybenzamine (a sympathetic blocking agent) can also be useful; some patients require invasive anesthesia by regional block.

questions.question_text: The police bring an acutely paranoid patient who was found wandering the streets into the emergency room. In your initial approach to this patient you should first:

options.text: Sedate the patient with haloperidol and lorazepam
Assess the dangerousness of the patient to self or others
Contact the patient's family if possible
Obtain any old charts from medical records

correct_answer.text: Assess the dangerousness of the patient to self or others

correct_answers.text: Assess the dangerousness of the patient to self or others

questions.explanation: In the situation in which you are presented with an unknown psychotic or paranoid patient, the first step is to make sure that the patient and staff are safe. All other options are valid but would be taken after an initial assessment of the patient's safety has been made. When given a question such as this on an examination, maintenance of safety comes first, and diagnosis and treatment come later. You would not automatically give sedation to the patient if he or she were not agitated or dangerous, so answer choice A is not the correct first move. Remember that past violence is the best predictor of future violence.

questions.question_text: Carbamazepine will not lower the levels or the efficacy of which one of the following agents?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is an inducer of CYP 2C19 and 3A4. It can therefore induce the metabolism of any substrate of the 2C19 and 3A4 systems. The 3A4 substrates that can be induced by carbamazepine include erythromycin, clarithromycin, alprazolam, diazepam, midazolam, cyclosporine, indinavir, ritonavir, saquinavir, diltiazem, nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil, atorvastatin, simvastatin, aripiprazole, buspirone, haloperidol, tamoxifen, trazodone, propranolol, zolpidem, zaleplon, methadone, estradiol (oral contraceptives), progesterone, testosterone, and fentanyl, to name but a few. The 2C19 substrates that can be induced by carbamazepine include amitriptyline, citalopram, clomipramine, imipramine, R-warfarin, propranolol, and primidone. Carbamazepine can lower lamotrigine levels by induction of glucuronidation enzyme 1A4. Clozapine is a substrate of CYP 1A2 and is not affected by carbamazepine.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is false concerning the right to die and surrogate decision making?

options.text: Patients who believe that continuing treatment would lessen their quality of life have the right to demand that treatment be withheld or withdrawn
Advanced directives or a living will is a way for patients to express their preferences before anything happens that would cause them to lose capacity
If a patient leaves no clear instructions, the state will carry out a course of action to protect and preserve human life
Surrogate decision makers can be appointed by the patient or the courts
The standard of substituted judgment means that the surrogate will do whatever is in the patient's best interests

correct_answer.text: The standard of substituted judgment means that the surrogate will do whatever is in the patient's best interests

correct_answers.text: The standard of substituted judgment means that the surrogate will do whatever is in the patient's best interests

questions.explanation: The standard of substituted judgment holds that a surrogate decision-maker will make decisions based on what the patient would have wanted and implies that the decision-maker be familiar with the patient's values and attitudes. The best interest principle, which was the past but not current standard, states that a decision-maker will decide which option would be in the patient's best interests. Patients do have the right to refuse treatment that they feel would lessen their quality of life. Advanced directives and living wills are ways for patients to preserve their wishes in writing so that their desires are reflected in the decisions that are made for them should they become incapacitated. The state will follow the course that preserves human life should a suitable surrogate decision-maker not be present. Surrogate decision-makers can be appointed by the patient, the court, or the hospital, often the patient's next of kin.

questions.question_text: Patients who smoke tobacco heavily can markedly reduce levels of psychotropic medications they are taking. Which one of the following medications is not affected by tobacco smoking in this way?
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoking is a potent inducer of CYP 1A2. As such, it can significantly lower levels of amitriptyline, fluvoxamine, clozapine, olanzapine, haloperidol, and imipramine. Risperidone is a substrate of CYP 2D6, and its levels can be lowered by 2D6 inducers such as dexamethasone and rifampin. Risperidone levels can be significantly increased by 2D6 inhibitors such as bupropion, citalopram, clomipramine, doxepin, duloxetine, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, and perphenazine. Risperidone levels are not affected by tobacco smoking.

questions.question_text: A consultation-liaison psychiatrist is called to evaluate a patient who is in denial of a major illness. The most important obligation of the psychiatrist at the first evaluation is to:

options.text: Tell the staff to 'play along' with the patient's denial
Make sure the patient has been informed about the illness and treatment

correct_answer.text: Make sure the patient has been informed about the illness and treatment

correct_answers.text: Make sure the patient has been informed about the illness and treatment

questions.explanation: One cannot treat what is assumed to be denial before actually knowing that it is denial. Often in medical settings things are not clearly explained to patients in language they can understand. As such, it is first necessary to explain what is going on to the patient clearly and in language he or she can follow. Confronting the patient's denial forcefully, and aggressively removing his or her defenses against overwhelming emotion, is potentially more harmful than helpful. Playing along with the denial can lead to noncompliance and failed treatment outcomes and is a bad idea. Neuropsychological testing is not necessary if a patient is in denial (unless a neurocognitive deficit precludes understanding, which was not the case here). Meeting the family is important, but not more important than making sure the patient has had the situation explained properly. Informing the family while the patient is left in the dark is not the best approach.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old delivers twins by uncomplicated caesarean section at 37 weeks. The pregnancy, her first, was unremarkable. On day 3 after her delivery, she experiences an acute onset of what she describes as the worst headache of her life. The neurologist is called and discovers that she has a notable bitemporal hemianopsia, neck stiffness, a positive Kernig's sign, persistent hypotension, and a right third nerve palsy. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: This is a classic case of Sheehan's syndrome, essentially a postpartum pituitary infarction or apoplexy. Classic symptoms resemble a pituitary hemorrhage. The pituitary infarction can cause chiasmal compression leading to bitemporal hemianopsia from bilateral medial optic nerve compression. Hypotension can be caused by a preexisting ACTH deficiency. The clinical picture can resemble subarachnoid hemorrhage from a berry aneurysm or AVM, accounting for severe acute headache and cranial nerve palsy; the syndrome can also cause meningeal irritation with positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs and stiff neck. Diagnosis often confirmed by CT or MRI. Treatment is generally supportive, with corticosteroid replacement or surgical decompression in certain cases. Cushing's disease is caused by endogenous ACTH overproduction from the anterior pituitary; Cushing's syndrome results from excessive exogenous or endogenous corticosteroids, with hypertension, truncal obesity, glucose intolerance, menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne, striae, osteoporosis, thin skin, proximal myopathy; dexamethasone suppression test is diagnostic. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most often from intracranial aneurysmal rupture, presenting with sudden explosive headache, meningeal signs, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, obtundation; head CT is imaging test of choice (90-95% sensitive within 24 hours, dropping to 80% after 72 hours); negative CT should be followed by LP for xanthochromia; cerebral angiography determines aneurysm location; interventions include endovascular coiling, microsurgical clipping, balloon embolization; 80-85% of aneurysms are anterior circulation. Bacterial meningitis presents with febrile illness, headache, stiff neck, cerebral dysfunction in over 85% of patients; CSF shows high opening pressure, high protein, decreased glucose, marked pleocytosis with PMNs; Neisseria meningitidis in children, Streptococcus pneumoniae in adults; treated with IV ampicillin, penicillin-G, third-generation cephalosporins. Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM) is a rare autosomal dominant migraine subtype mapped to chromosome 19p13, coding for the α1 subunit of a brain-specific calcium channel.

questions.question_text: A patient describes feeling anxious about being in places or situations from which escape may be difficult or in which help may not be available should the patient begin to panic. The patient avoids various situations because of these fears. The term that best describes this patient's symptoms is:
questions.explanation: The question stem accurately describes agoraphobia. The other answer choices are distractors: Agonothete is the judge of games in ancient Greece; Agoniada is the bark of a South American shrub; Agora is the market place in ancient Greece; Agouara is a South American wild dog or crab-eating raccoon.

questions.question_text: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus presents as the triad of:

options.text: Dementia, axial rigidity, and vertical ophthalmoplegia

questions.explanation: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) presents with the triad of dementia, incontinence, and gait disturbance. The cause in up to one-third of cases is undetermined; NPH can be caused by trauma, infection, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Brain CT/MRI reveal enlargement of the third, fourth, and lateral ventricles. NPH causes an apraxic (magnetic) gait; dementia is considered subcortical (slowing of verbal/motor functioning with intact cortical functions); abulia, apathy, and depression are common; urinary incontinence occurs early, particularly with gait disturbance; lumbar puncture reveals normal opening pressure. Serial lumbar punctures with CSF drainage can improve symptoms and support the diagnosis. Ventriculoperitoneal shunting is the treatment of choice, successful in up to 80% of cases; shunts fail about one-third of the time, with complications including subdural hematoma and infection. Diffuse Lewy-body disease is the second-most prevalent dementia after Alzheimer's, with the triad of dementia, parkinsonism, and visual hallucinations; hallmark is extreme sensitivity to dopamine receptor antagonists; hallucinations are ideally treated with newer antipsychotics (quetiapine, clozapine, ziprasidone); rivastigmine/donepezil may help cognition. Wernicke's encephalopathy presents with acute triad of mental confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and gait ataxia, predominantly in alcoholic patients, with periventricular hemorrhages on autopsy and MRI abnormalities in periaqueductal regions, mammillary bodies, and medial thalami. Sydenham's chorea is a result of rheumatic fever, extremely rare now, more frequent in girls 5-15 years; chorea begins insidiously and lasts up to 6 months; anti-basal ganglia antibodies detected by Western blot; valproic acid is useful therapy.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not true concerning cyclothymic disorder?

options.text: It is similar to bipolar disorder but less severe
Symptoms must be present for at least 2 years
It is equally common in men and women
Substance abuse is common in patients with cyclothymia
There are often psychotic symptoms found in patients with cyclothymia

correct_answer.text: There are often psychotic symptoms found in patients with cyclothymia

correct_answers.text: There are often psychotic symptoms found in patients with cyclothymia

questions.explanation: Cyclothymic disorder does not involve psychotic symptoms, although these symptoms may be found in bipolar disorder. Cyclothymia is a less severe form of bipolar, with alternation between hypomania and moderate depression. Symptoms must exist for 2 years to make the diagnosis. It is equally common in men and women. Substance use often coexists. The onset is usually insidious and occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood. Lifetime prevalence of cyclothymia is 0.5% to 6.3%.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a potential risk factor for ischemic stroke?
questions.explanation: Depression is not considered a stroke risk factor.
